newsitem.title: QATAR: Yamani sees prolonged weak oil price.
newsitem.headline: Yamani sees prolonged weak oil price.

text.p: Former Saudi oil minister Sheikh Ahmed Zaki Yamani on Monday warned of persistent weak oil prices up to the end of the decade because of higher crude flows from both OPEC and non-OPEC producers.

"Looking beyond 1997 towards the turn of the century, there is a strong likelihood that oil prices will remain weak, despite strong growth in oil demand," Yamani said in a speech delivered to a gas conference here.
"The basic reason for this is the sheer volume of additional oil supplies that is likely to be available from non-OPEC and OPEC countries alike," Yamani said in his paper.
Yamani, who steered oil policy in the world's largest oil producer and exporter for 24 years until 1986, placed special blame at the feet of OPEC producers who ignored output quotas.
"Some OPEC member countries are behaving as if they do not belong to the organisation. They tend to produce every barrel they can," said Yamani.
Current production from OPEC's 11 members is running at more than 26.5 million barrels per day (bpd) according to independent assessments, way in excess of its agreed ceiling of 25.03 million bpd.

Yamani questioned how long OPEC heavywights Saudi Arabia, United Arab Emirates and Kuwait -- who have kept to quota levels despite having additional spare capacity -- would tolerate over-production by some members.
"The three countries...have been tolerant because oil prices were high enough. Will they be prepared to be so indulgent when oil prices drop to, say, $16 a barrel or below," Yamani said.
"One way of discipling recalcitrant members is by flooding the market and this could indeed happen," he said.

Yamani orchestrated a policy in the mid-eighties of turning up Saudi oil taps in order to deter higher prices advocated by price "hawks" such as Libya and Algeria. The action resulted in a glut and a severe fall in oil prices in 1985 to below $9.
Oil prices have hovered this year above $20.
